To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months was associated with a significantly lower risk for HIV-1 transmission compared with mixed feeding, but not compared with no breastfeeding.
the risk of early mother tochild transmission of HIV 2 was lower in infants who were exclusively breastfed than in those who were mixed fed.

exclusive breastfeeding for 3 months is associated with a significantly lower risk (p<0*05) of early mother to infant HIV 1 transmission (14% vs 24%) than mixed feeding (p=0.03) or no breastfeeding (p=0:5) after adjustment for potential confounding variables.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of infant feeding patterns (breastfeeding, mixed feeding, and formula feeding) on early mother to infant transmission of HIV 19.
the impact of infant feeding practices on the transmission of HIV from infected women to their infants.
the impact of infant feeding practices on the transmission of HIV 2 from mother to child.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study shows a significantly lower risk for HIV transmission in exclusively breastfed children than in children receiving mixed feeding and that the risk is similar in exclusively breastfed and never breastfed children.
exclusive breastfeeding is associated with a reduced risk of early mother to infant transmission of HIV 2.

exclusive breastfeeding may offer women in developing countries a culturally acceptable and effective means of preventing HIV 1 transmission to their infants while maintaining the overwhelming health benefits of breastfeeding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of transmission is lower in exclusively breastfed children compared to those receiving mixed feeding.
the pattern of breastfeeding (exclusive vs mixed) was a critical determinant of the risk of early mother tochild transmission of HIV 11.

exclusive breastfeeding for 3 months is associated with a significantly lower risk for mother to child transmission than mixed feeding and that the risk for transmission was similar to that in infants who never received breast milk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
breastfeeding can be a safe way to feed babies in developing countries.
exclusive breastfeeding is a safe option for HIV 1 positive women in developing countries and that it reduces mother to child transmission rates.
exclusive breastfeeding is a good strategy for HIV positive moms.
